implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library is the mechanism: the OpenSSL module "provides SSL, TLS and general purpose cryptography" and wraps OpenSSL, offering OpenSSL::Cipher with named ciphers ("aes-256-cbc", "aes-256-gcm"), OpenSSL::Digest, PKCS5 for password-based derivation, and SecureRandom for keys and nonces ("an interface to secure random number generators which are suitable for generating session keys"). The realization: name a standard cipher and mode in code, generate key material with SecureRandom or import it from a secret store, and let the OpenSSL module do the work; a hand-written cipher, a base64 "encryption" helper, or a secret committed to the repository is the inversion. Rails' ActiveSupport::MessageEncryptor/MessageVerifier is the framework-level form of the same idea.
code_sketch:
cipher = OpenSSL::Cipher.new('aes-256-gcm')           # published algorithm, named
cipher.encrypt
cipher.key = SecureRandom.bytes(32)                   # secret from a CSPRNG
iv = SecureRandom.random_bytes(12)                    # public nonce
cipher.iv = iv
data = cipher.update(plaintext) + cipher.final
tag = cipher.auth_tag
pitfalls: Kernel#rand / Random for tokens and nonces uses a non-cryptographic generator; session keys, IVs and tokens must come from SecureRandom (or OpenSSL::Random).
The OpenSSL module raises when a secure RNG is unavailable; rescuing that and falling back to a weaker source reverses the rule.

Credentials committed or stored in plain files (config/secrets.yml, a checked-in .env) are public once the repository is; use encrypted credentials or a secret manager - and the encryption key must not live in the same artifact.
